native_result.query: In which domain do the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies?
native_result.HypoA: In Experimental Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies with ratio of males in original and replication studies being and 0.87 and 0.84 respectively.
native_result.HypoB: In the domain of Economics, the majority of authors tend to be male for both original and replication studies: 10 of 18 Economics O/R pairs (55.6%) are majority-male on both sides (authors_male.o > 0.5 AND authors_male.r > 0.5), versus 36.7% in Cognitive (18/49) and 27.0% in Social (20/74), and an all-discipline base rate of 34.0% (48/141). Economics also has the highest single-side majorities (original 77.8%, replication 72.2%). The result is robust to the tie rule: under the 'at least half' (>=0.5) variant Economics still leads (83.3% vs 61.2% Cognitive, 56.8% Social). Caveat: the Economics estimate rests on only 18 pairs, all from the Experimental Economics (ee) replication project, so it is a small-N finding, though it clearly stands out from the overall base rate.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded the raw study dataset (927 rows x 57 cols). Deduplicated to 141 unique O/R pairs (id): kept aggregated=True rows for ml1/ml3 (26 pooled replication-team rows) and the single rows for ee/rpp (115). Computed majority-male flags for both rules (>0.5 strict, >=0.5 sensitivity) on authors_male.o and authors_male.r, formed the conjunction flag, and tabulated counts/shares per discipline plus the all-discipline base rate. Diagnostics: 0.5 ties (33 o-side, 27 r-side pairs), drop=True pair handling (robustness, n=131, winner unchanged), and pair-level output table saved. The Fisher-z replication-success file was inspected and excluded (no author-gender columns).
